questions.prompt: Your module asks you to design a poster carrying a motto, and it prints two of them: "If it's not far, don't go by car" and "Do it right, switch off the light". What do both of them do?

options.text: They ask a question that the reader has to answer.
They give an instruction, and they end on a rhyme.
They name the person who ought to act.
They state a figure that the reader can go and check.

questions.explanation: A motto has to stay in the head, and these two do it the same way. Each is an instruction — don't go by car, switch off the light — and each closes on a rhyme, far with car and right with light, so that half of it brings the other half back. Neither asks anything: they tell the reader what to do. Neither names anybody either, and that is deliberate — an instruction with nobody's name on it is addressed to whoever reads it. And neither gives a figure; a motto that had to be checked before it could be believed would stop working as a motto.

questions.prompt: A neighbour cannot lift the sandbags alone. You see her from the gate, and you decide there and then to help her. What do you say?

options.text: I am helping you with those.
I help you with those.
I'm going to help you with those.
I'll help you with those.

questions.explanation: An offer made at the moment of speaking takes will, which is your book's third use of the form — its own example is "If you need that medicine now, I'll get it for you." be going to announces a plan formed earlier, and you formed nothing: you have only just seen her from the gate. The present continuous states an arrangement already fixed with somebody. And the plain present states a habit, which would make you the person who lifts her sandbags every day.

questions.prompt: A rescue team reaches a flooded village at dawn. Its leader looks at the mud line left on the walls and writes in his notebook: "The river must have risen in the night." What is he doing with that sentence?

options.text: He is concluding that the river rose in the night.
He is concluding that the river is still rising this morning.
He is ordering his team to measure the river.
He is promising to warn the village next time.

questions.explanation: must followed by have and a past participle draws a conclusion about something that was already over before the conclusion was drawn — and the evidence for it is what he can see now, the mud line on the walls. Nobody watched the water rise; he works it out. A conclusion about this morning would be must be rising, with must in front of a base form, and the sentence does not say that. The order and the promise both read must as the modal of obligation, and the past of that must is had to, not must have.

questions.prompt: One of the headlines of your module states what happens to a tsunami when it reaches shallower water near the coast. What does it say?

options.text: It breaks up before it reaches the shore.
It keeps the same speed and the same height.
It loses speed, and its height grows.
It loses height, and its speed grows.

questions.explanation: The headline is worth learning because it says the opposite of what most people expect: a tsunami loses speed when it reaches shallower water, but its height grows. Out at sea the wave runs fast and lies so low that a ship may not notice it; over the shelf near the coast the sea bed holds it back, and the water that was spread through the whole depth has nowhere left to go but up. The version that reverses the two — height lost, speed gained — is the picture people carry in their heads, and it is wrong on both counts. Nothing in the module says the wave breaks up before it arrives, and a wave that kept the same speed and the same height would not be a disaster at all.

questions.prompt: Read: "The village was flooded because the dam gave way." Which sentence keeps the same cause and the same effect?

options.text: The dam gave way, so the village was flooded.
The dam gave way because the village was flooded.
The village was flooded, so the dam gave way.
The village was flooded although the dam gave way.

questions.explanation: because looks back at the cause and so looks forward to the effect, so changing one word for the other means changing the halves over as well. The dam is the cause and the flood is the effect in the original, and only one rewrite keeps them that way: the dam gave way, so the village was flooded. The two sentences that put the flood first now make the flood the cause and the dam the effect, one of them with so and the other with because — the same reversal twice over, and in each case a village would have had to flood before its dam broke. And although abandons cause and effect altogether: it announces a contrast, and would claim the village flooded in spite of the dam.

questions.prompt: A classmate tells you that his uncle's family lost their house and their boat in the flood. Three of these replies do what the section asks of you. The fourth is meant kindly and lands badly. Which one should you not say?

options.text: My heart goes out to them.
I'm so sorry to hear that.
At least they still have each other.
If there is anything I can do, tell me.

questions.explanation: Sympathy is said to a person, briefly, and it does not look for a bright side: "At least they still have each other." tells somebody who has just lost a house and a livelihood that things are not so bad, which is not what he came to hear, however kindly it is meant. It could have been worse does the same thing and lands the same way. The three others are the language of the section. "My heart goes out to them." is the one formula the article at the end of the reading actually prints, about all those who lost loved ones and livelihoods. "I'm so sorry to hear that." is the short spoken form, beside That must be dreadful for you and Please accept my sympathy. And "If there is anything I can do, tell me." offers something concrete, which is what the family in the passage themselves did with a fund and boats for the fishermen. Note what none of the four does: judge the news. That is a different job, and a different set of phrases.
